title: Balance Sheet: Meaning, Format and a Worked Example
excerpt: Learn what a balance sheet shows with a fictional statement, the assets-equal-liabilities-plus-equity equation and a practical review checklist.

body.text: Balance sheet meaning: it is a statement, also called a statement of financial position in some reporting frameworks, that presents an entity's assets liabilities and equity at a particular date. Its core relationship is Assets = Liabilities + Equity. A balance sheet format and its line items, disclosures and terminology depend on the entity and applicable accounting framework. The figures below are invented and simplified for learning; they are not a statutory template or a real company's financial information.
The three parts of a balance sheet

items: Assets are resources recognised by the entity under the applicable framework, such as cash, receivables, inventory or equipment.
Liabilities are obligations recognised by the entity, such as amounts payable or borrowings, subject to the applicable recognition rules.
Equity represents the residual interest after liabilities are deducted from assets; its composition and presentation vary by entity type and framework.

body.text: Imagine a fictional small business at 31 March. It has cash of ₹40,000, inventory of ₹20,000, receivables of ₹30,000 and equipment of ₹110,000. Total illustrative assets are ₹200,000. It owes ₹70,000 to suppliers and lenders combined, and has equity of ₹130,000. Liabilities plus equity total ₹200,000, matching assets. A simple learning worksheet could show each line, its supporting schedule, the statement date, the currency and a review status. This example leaves out many real-world recognition, valuation, classification and disclosure questions.

items: Cash — ₹40,000: a fictional cash balance at the statement date.
Inventory — ₹20,000: an illustrative recognised balance; real valuation follows the entity's accounting framework and policy.
Receivables — ₹30,000: fictional amounts due, subject to applicable recognition and measurement rules.
Equipment — ₹110,000: an illustrative asset amount; real statements may include depreciation and other adjustments.
Liabilities — ₹70,000 combined: a simplified total for amounts owed to suppliers and lenders.
Equity — ₹130,000: the balancing residual in this example, not a valuation of an owner's interest.

body.text: A complete line-by-line view of the fictional example

items: Assets: cash INR 40,000 + inventory INR 20,000 + receivables INR 30,000 + equipment INR 110,000 = INR 200,000.
Liabilities: supplier payables INR 25,000 + bank borrowing INR 45,000 = INR 70,000.
Equity: owner capital INR 100,000 + retained earnings INR 30,000 = INR 130,000.
Equation check: liabilities INR 70,000 + equity INR 130,000 = assets INR 200,000.

body.text: The earlier summary groups the obligations and equity for readability; this breakdown shows how the totals reconcile. These invented figures do not prescribe whether a real balance is current or non-current, how it should be measured, or what disclosures are required.
Common balance-sheet classification and review errors

items: Counting a balance in both a sub-ledger and a summary line, which overstates the total.
Netting receivables against payables without confirming that applicable rules and facts permit the presentation.
Treating an overdue receivable as collectible without reviewing support and the entity's applicable measurement policy.
Calling a borrowing long-term based only on an intention to refinance, without checking the contract and applicable classification requirements.
Reviewing a balance-sheet date as though it covered a whole period; income and cash-flow statements report activity over a period.

body.text: A balance sheet is a snapshot at a date, not a complete explanation of performance or cash movement. An income statement reports results over a period, while a cash-flow statement reports cash flows under the applicable rules. To understand a business, readers generally need the statements together, their notes, comparative information and relevant context. A balanced equation alone does not show whether assets are recoverable, obligations are complete or classifications are appropriate.

items: Confirm the reporting entity, statement date, currency, accounting framework and whether figures are standalone or consolidated.
Read the notes and accounting policies for material balances, estimates, commitments and classifications.
Compare periods carefully and investigate large movements instead of assuming that a change is automatically good or bad.
Check how figures connect to supporting ledgers or schedules and whether appropriate review and approval occurred.
Do not treat this simplified example as an investment signal, credit assessment or substitute for professional advice.
